extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato / political philosophy; people studying qualities of rulers and philosophers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and lists the qualities, faculties, and social/practical standards Plato (Republic, Book VI) uses to identify genuine philosophers and to argue who should rule. Includes virtues, cognitive capacities, anti-patterns (sophists, corruption), and suitability for governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lover of the vision of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are lovers of the vision of truth (true philosophers) as opposed to mere lovers of sights and sounds or imitators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato contrasts genuine philosophers—'lovers of the vision of truth'—with imitators and lovers of opinion. Genuine philosophers seek the eternal and unchangeable rather than the manifold; this love of truth underpins all other qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to apprehend absolute beauty (the Form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Few are able to attain to the sight of absolute beauty; a true philosopher can distinguish the idea (Form) from the objects which participate in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: those fond of fine tones, colours, and forms who cannot see absolute beauty are mere lovers of sights and sounds. A philosopher must not put copies in place of the real object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge versus opinion (cognitive faculty distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is a faculty relative to being (the eternal); opinion is a distinct faculty concerned with the intermediate, the many which are neither pure being nor pure non-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers must possess knowledge (about being) rather than mere opinion; evaluate whether a person seeks and attains knowledge of essences rather than mere opinion about appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness (hatred of falsehood)
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher 'will never intentionally receive into their mind falsehood' and will love the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is non-negotiable: a true lover of wisdom 'must' love truth. Anti-pattern: loving falsehood or being comfortable with false beliefs disqualifies one as a true philosopher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance / disinclination to bodily pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: The true philosopher's desires are drawn toward knowledge and the pleasures of the soul; he will 'hardly feel bodily pleasure' and be temperate and the reverse of covetous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the individual prioritises intellectual/spiritual pleasures over bodily ones; excessive sensual desire indicates lack of the philosophical nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence of mind / absence of meanness (illiberality)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be 'no secret corner of illiberality'; meanness is antagonistic to a soul that longs after the whole of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A philosophical nature is grand, open, and liberal; pettiness or stinginess in character is an anti-pattern and incompatible with true philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage is among the natural gifts of the philosopher; he will not account death as fearful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage here is moral and intellectual steadiness—fearlessness in pursuit of truth. Cowardice disqualifies a person from being a true philosopher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice and gentleness
rubrics_metrics.description: A harmoniously constituted philosopher 'can never be unjust or hard in his dealings'—justice and gentleness are signs that mark the philosophical nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate interpersonal conduct for fairness and softness; harshness and injustice indicate lack of true philosophical disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in learning / intrinsic love of study
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher has a pleasure in learning; no one will love that which gives them pain and in which after much toil they make little progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine philosopher pursues study for its own sake and enjoys it; reluctance or dislike for learning is a disqualifier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good memory
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher 'should have a good memory'—a soul which forgets cannot be ranked among genuine philosophic natures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retention of learning and the ability to recall is an important faculty; being forgetful makes philosophical study fruitless (an 'empty vessel').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quickness / aptitude to learn
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher should be 'quick to learn'—one of the natural gifts (alongside memory, courage, magnificence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess rapid intellectual uptake and facility in learning; slow or laborious learners lacking perseverance are less suited to true philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonious, well-proportioned, gracious mind
rubrics_metrics.description: A naturally well-proportioned and gracious mind, inclined spontaneously towards the true being of everything, is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportion and harmony in character (not disjointed or inharmonious) are positive indicators; inharmonious or disproportionate natures are less fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from covetousness, boasting, and meanness
rubrics_metrics.description: A true philosopher is not covetous, not a boaster, not mean or cowardly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material greed, vanity, and petty character traits undermine the love of truth; presence of these is an anti-pattern often exploited by corrupting influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not rendered useless by external honours or flatterers
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the philosophic nature may make one conspicuous and admired in youth, genuine philosophers must not be diverted by honours, flatterers, or the prospect of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: early honours can lead to pride and away from study; a true philosopher must remain humble and committed despite social adulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability and fitness to govern (guardian suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who grasp eternal and unchangeable truths are the ones 'who should be the rulers of our State'—whichever of the two classes are best able to guard the laws and institutions should be guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governance suitability is judged by capacity to know the true nature of justice, beauty, and good and to order laws accordingly, not by popularity or rhetorical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to corruption by wealth, beauty, rank, and externals
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary goods of life—beauty, wealth, strength, rank and connections—have a corrupting and distracting effect; the finest natures are most sensitive to alien conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate environment and influences: even high natural gifts may become sources of corruption without proper nurture and education. Safeguards are necessary to preserve philosophic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-pandering to popular opinion (not a sophist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophists teach the opinion of the many, learning to discern and please the mob's tastes; a true philosopher does not base wisdom on what the crowd delights in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: conforming craftsmanship or public-flattering (producing what the crowd praises) indicates sophist-like education, not true wisdom. The pilot parable exemplifies the danger of letting sailors (the mob) choose the helmsman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the whole/essence rather than the many particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The true lover of knowledge strives after being as a whole and the true nature of every essence rather than the multiplicity of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the individual's inquiry aims at essences/Forms (unity) rather than merely manipulating or praising particular instances or appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of social misrecognition (philosophers seen as useless)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers will often be regarded by the many as 'useless' or 'good-for-nothings' because they do not pander to public taste and often focus on things invisible to the crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical consideration: one should expect hostility or misunderstanding from popular opinion; it is not a moral failing of the philosopher but of the public.
